nameStory: The "whiteface" part of this dragonfly's name comes from the distinctive white or pale coloring on its face, which stands out like a bright mask against its darker body. The "crimson-ringed" refers to the reddish bands that encircle its abdomen, creating striking rings of color that catch the eye when it's perched on a sunny reed or branch.
description: The Crimson-ringed Whiteface is a medium-sized dragonfly that belongs to the skimmer family, one of the most common dragonfly groups you'll encounter. Like all dragonflies, it has four clear wings that it holds out perpendicular to its body when at rest, and large compound eyes that give it excellent vision for hunting small flying insects. Its body is dark with distinctive reddish rings around the abdomen, and its face has the characteristic white or pale coloring that gives whitefaces their name. These dragonflies are strong fliers that often perch on vegetation near water, making them relatively easy to observe and photograph.

idTips.label: White Face
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive white or pale yellowish face that contrasts sharply with the dark head - it looks like the dragonfly is wearing a bright mask

idTips.label: Crimson Rings
idTips.description: The abdomen shows reddish or crimson bands that wrap around like belts, most visible when the dragonfly is perched in good sunlight

idTips.label: Dark Body
idTips.description: The overall body appears dark brown to black, creating strong contrast with both the white face and red abdominal rings

idTips.label: Clear Wings
idTips.description: Wings are typically clear and unmarked, held straight out from the body when perched, with a slight amber tinge at the bases

idTips.label: Perching Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen perching on the tips of reeds, grasses, or low shrubs near water, returning repeatedly to the same favorite spots

habitat: Crimson-ringed Whitefaces are found around cool, northern waters including bogs, fens, small ponds, and slow-moving streams, particularly in areas with sphagnum moss and sedges. In New England, they prefer higher elevation locations and are more common in the northern regions of Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine. Look for them in areas where the water is slightly acidic and surrounded by coniferous forests or mixed woodland edges.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, typically May, when you might spot them making their first flights near breeding waters. Early individuals may appear sluggish in cool morning temperatures.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs from June through August when adults are most active, hunting and mating. This is the best time for identification as their colors are most vibrant and they're most likely to be perched visibly.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases significantly by September, with only occasional sightings of late-season individuals. Most adults die off with the first hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: No adults are present; the species overwinters as larvae (nymphs) in the water, buried in bottom sediments or hiding among aquatic vegetation.

funFact: Dragonflies like the Crimson-ringed Whiteface are aerial acrobats with a 95% hunting success rate - higher than sharks, lions, or any other predator on Earth, thanks to their ability to predict exactly where their prey will be and intercept it mid-flight!
confusionNotes: This species can be confused with other whitefaces, but the crimson rings are the key distinguisher - Dot-tailed Whitefaces have spots rather than rings, while Frosted Whitefaces have a more powdery, less distinctly ringed appearance. Memory trick: "Crimson rings around the middle, like red belts on a white-faced wrestler."
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name "glacialis" refers to this species' preference for cooler, northern climates - it's actually more common in Canada and Alaska than in New England, making any sighting here somewhat special for dragonfly enthusiasts.
compareHints: Among New England's whitefaces, the Crimson-ringed is distinguished by its bold red abdominal rings, while the Dot-tailed has yellow spots, the Frosted appears more powdery white, and the Hudsonian has more subdued markings. The Belted Whiteface is most similar but has a broader white belt across the abdomen rather than multiple narrow red rings.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's whitefaces, the dot-tailed whiteface is distinguished by its spotted abdomen pattern.
Compared to its whiteface relatives, the frosted whiteface is distinguished by the mature male's chalky, pruinose coating that's more extensive than in other species.
Among the whitefaces, Hudsonian Whitefaces are distinguished mainly by habitat preference rather than dramatic physical differences.

Among New England's whitefaces, the Belted is the only one with that distinctive red belt around its waist - other whitefaces like the Dot-tailed have spots or different markings but lack this wraparound band.
